pages.hook: In many American homes, the kitchen is the center of the house. Friends talk, kids help, and everyone ends up standing near the stove.
pages.polite: When you help in someone else's kitchen, ask first: **“Can I help?”** Then listen to the steps.

mythfact.s: American recipes often use cups and tablespoons.
mythfact.why: Many US recipes measure by volume: a cup of flour, a tablespoon of oil.

mythfact.s: American ovens use degrees Celsius.
mythfact.why: Ovens in the USA use degrees Fahrenheit, for example 350°F.

mythfact.s: A guest can ask “Can I help?” in the kitchen.
mythfact.why: It is friendly and normal, and hosts often say yes.

mythfact.s: You should touch a pan to see if it is hot.
mythfact.why: Never touch it. Say “Careful! The pan is hot!” and use a pot holder.

lines: 2. Cut 1 onion. Fry it in a pan.
3. Add 2 tomatoes and a pinch of salt.

decode.q: What do you do after you cut the onion?
decode.why: Step 2 says: “Fry it in a pan.”

compare.br: In Brazil many home cooks measure by eye and use grams, liters and a fogão with a gas flame.
compare.us: In the USA recipes often say cups, tablespoons and Fahrenheit, and many homes have an electric or gas stove.
compare.tip: When you read an American recipe, check the unit first: cup, tablespoon or degrees F.
compare.ask: What is one dish you can cook? Say the first two steps in English.

quiz.q: You want to help a friend cook. You say…
quiz.why: Can I help? is the polite offer.

quiz.q: The pan is very hot. You say…
A recipe says “350°F”. What is it about?
quiz.why: °F means degrees Fahrenheit, used for oven heat.

pages.title: Reading quest — Pasta night with my roommate · part 1
text: On Sunday night, my roommate Aaron and I cooked together in our small kitchen. He opened the fridge and asked, “**What are you making?**” I smiled and said, “**Pasta with tomato sauce**.”

Aaron wanted to help. “**Can I help?**” he asked. “**Sure**,” I said. “**Cut the onions, please**.” He took a knife and a cutting board. “**How many?**” he asked. “**Just one**,” I said. “Then **add the tomatoes**.”
I put a big pan on the stove and added some oil and a little salt. The kitchen smelled so good! Aaron came near the stove, and I said, “**Careful! The pan is hot**.” He stepped back and laughed.

fast.why: The writer and Aaron cook pasta at home.

scan.q: How many onions does the writer ask for?
What does the writer say when the pan is hot?
What does Aaron say at the end?

tf.s: The writer warns Aaron about the hot pan.

tf.why: They eat at the small table at home.

order: Aaron asks what the writer is making.
Aaron cuts one onion.
The writer adds salt to the pan.
The writer warns about the hot pan.
They sit and eat dinner.

ctx.why: Stepped back = moved away from something.

ctx.sent: The food was simple, but it was delicious.

pages.title: Reading quest — Pasta night with my roommate · part 2
text: My family always says that cooking is like a game. First you cut, then you fry, next you add, and finally you taste. I thought about the fairy tale The Magic Porridge Pot, with a small pot that cooks porridge by magic. We have no magic pot, but tonight we made pasta, and it was a lot of fun.

When the sauce was ready, I put the pasta on two plates. Aaron looked at his plate and said, “**Dinner is served!**” We sat at the small table and ate slowly. The food was simple, but it was delicious.
